title: Chemical Kinetics

toc.title: 9.1 Rate of reaction, rate expressions, the rate constant and its units; order and molecularity
9.2 Integrated rate laws and half-lives of zero- and first-order reactions
9.3 Collision theory, activation and threshold energy, the activated complex; factors affecting rate; catalysis

html:
Stoichiometry tells you what a reaction produces; kinetics tells you how fast it gets there.

The paper carries about one question from this chapter, and it is nearly always one of three things: a definition that turns on the difference between order and molecularity, a one-line calculation with t_{1/2} or the integrated rate law, or a statement about catalysts and collision theory that is true except for one wrong word.

Almost every mark here is lost to a sign, a unit or a half-life taken as proportional to concentration.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Rate of reaction is a positive quantity: for a reactant, rate = -\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[A]}{dt}; average rate uses a finite interval, instantaneous rate the tangent.
  • Rate law is experimental; order = m+n can be zero, fractional or negative. Molecularity is theoretical and always a whole number.
  • Units of k: order 0 → mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; order 1 → s⁻¹; order 2 → L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; order n → mol^{1-n} L^{n-1} s⁻¹.
  • Zero order: [A] = [A]_0 - kt, t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k. First order: \ln([A]_0/[A]) = kt, t_{1/2} = 0.693/k — independent of [A]_0.
  • A straight line of \ln[A] against t proves first order; its slope is -k.
  • Collision theory: only collisions with energy ≥ threshold energy and the right orientation react; the activated complex sits at the top of the barrier.
  • Arrhenius: k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}; a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate because the fraction of molecules above E_a roughly doubles.
  • A catalyst lowers E_a for both directions equally: it changes the rate, never \Delta H, \Delta G or K.

9.1 Rate of reaction, rate expressions, the rate constant and its units; order and molecularity

Rate of reaction: average and instantaneous

Rate of reaction

The rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Because concentrations are measured in mol L⁻¹ and time in seconds, the unit is mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (also written mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ or M s⁻¹).

For a reactant the concentration falls, so \Delta[R] is negative. Rate must be positive, hence the minus sign:

\text{rate} = -\frac{\Delta[\text{R}]}{\Delta t}

For a product the concentration rises and no sign is needed. For the general equation aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD all four species must give the same number for the rate, so each is divided by its own coefficient:

\text{rate} = -\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[A]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{b}\frac{d[B]}{dt} = \frac{1}{c}\frac{d[C]}{dt} = \frac{1}{d}\frac{d[D]}{dt}

Reaction Rate expression
2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = \frac{1}{4}\frac{d[\text{NO}_2]}{dt} = \frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}
H₂ + I₂ → 2HI -\frac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{HI}]}{dt}
2HI → H₂ + I₂ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{HI}]}{dt} = \frac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt}
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ -\frac{d[\text{N}_2]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{3}\frac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt}

Average rate is measured over a finite interval, \Delta[R]/\Delta t, and is read from the slope of the chord joining two points on the concentration–time curve.

Instantaneous rate is the limit as \Delta t \rightarrow 0 and is the slope of the tangent at that instant.

Because the reactant is consumed fastest at the start, the average rate over the first interval is always larger than the instantaneous rate at the end of it.

Two mistakes that cost marks every year
  • The sign. "Rate of disappearance of N₂O₅" is a positive number; "rate of change of [N₂O₅]" is negative. If an option is negative and the stem says "rate of disappearance", it is wrong.
  • The coefficient. For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ the rate of formation of NO₂ is four times the rate of reaction, and the rate of disappearance of N₂O₅ is twice it. Do not report d[\text{NO}_2]/dt as "the rate".
Rate from one measured species

Problem. In the decomposition 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ the concentration of O₂ rises at 2.0 \times 10^{-3} mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find the rate of reaction and the rate of disappearance of N₂O₅.

Solution. O₂ has coefficient 1, so it reports the rate directly: rate = d[\text{O}_2]/dt = \mathbf{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. N₂O₅ has coefficient 2 and is consumed, so -d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]/dt = 2 \times \text{rate} = \mathbf{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Rate law and the rate constant

Rate law and rate constant

The rate law (rate expression) is an equation that relates the rate of a reaction to the concentrations of the reactants, with the exponents found by experiment: \text{rate} = k[A]^m[B]^n.

The constant k is the rate constant (specific reaction rate): the rate when every concentration in the law is 1 mol L⁻¹.

k does not change as the reaction proceeds, and it does not depend on the concentrations. It does depend on temperature, on the presence of a catalyst, and on the nature of the reactants and the solvent.

The units of k are whatever makes rate = k \times (concentration)^n come out in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. For overall order n:

\text{unit of } k = \text{mol}^{1-n}\,\text{L}^{n-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}

Overall order Rate law Unit of k
0 rate = k mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
1 rate = k[A] s⁻¹
2 rate = k[A]^2 or k[A][B] L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
3 rate = k[A]^2[B] L² mol⁻² s⁻¹
n rate = k[A]^n mol^{1-n} L^{n-1} s⁻¹
Getting the unit of k without memorising five rows

Take the rate law, put the unit mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ on the left and the concentration units on the right, and solve. For rate = k[A]^2: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ = (unit of k) × (mol L⁻¹)², so unit of k = L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

For a first-order reaction the same trick gives s⁻¹, which is why a first-order k is sometimes called the frequency of reaction.

Order and molecularity — the pair examiners love to confuse

Order and molecularity

The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the power to which its concentration is raised in the experimentally determined rate law; the overall order is the sum of these powers.

The molecularity of a reaction is the number of molecules (atoms or ions) that collide in a single elementary step to bring about the reaction.

Order Molecularity
How obtained experiment (rate law) from the mechanism (theory)
Value 0, 1, 2, 3, or a fraction; can be negative always a positive whole number, 1, 2 or 3
Applies to the reaction as a whole one elementary step only
Depends on concentration no no
Can change with conditions yes — a reaction can change order as concentration changes no
Relation order = molecularity only for a single-step reaction

Where they differ — learn these three.

Reaction Molecularity Experimental order Why
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl 2 1.5, rate = k[\text{H}_2][\text{Cl}_2]^{1/2} chain mechanism; the Cl₂ step is not the only slow one
2NH₃ → N₂ + 3H₂ on hot tungsten 2 0 the surface is saturated, so pressure no longer matters
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆ 2 1 (pseudo-first-order) water is in such large excess that its concentration hardly changes
Order is NOT read off the balanced equation

A balanced equation is a book-keeping statement about atoms, not a description of the slow step.

The decomposition 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ is first order, not second; the oxidation 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ is third order; and H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl is of order 1.5.

Any option that says "the order is the sum of the coefficients in the balanced equation" is wrong, and it is the most popular distractor in this chapter.

Finding the order from initial rates

Hold all concentrations but one constant and see how the rate responds.

Experiment [A] (M) [B] (M) Initial rate (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)
1 0.10 0.10 2.0 \times 10^{-3}
2 0.20 0.10 4.0 \times 10^{-3}
3 0.10 0.20 8.0 \times 10^{-3}

Experiments 1 → 2: [A] doubles, rate doubles, so the order in A is 1. Experiments 1 → 3: [B] doubles, rate becomes four times larger, so the order in B is 2. Overall order = 1 + 2 = 3, rate = k[A][B]^2.

Order, rate law and rate constant from a table

Problem. Use the table above. Find the rate law, the overall order and k.

Solution. Order in A: \frac{4.0}{2.0} = 2 = 2^m, so m = 1. Order in B: \frac{8.0}{2.0} = 4 = 2^n, so n = 2. Rate = k[A][B]^2, overall order 3.

From experiment 1: k = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{(0.10)(0.10)^2} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \mathbf{2.0} L² mol⁻² s⁻¹. The unit follows the overall order 3: mol^{1-3} L^{3-1} s⁻¹ = L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.

Two-second check on any order question

Ask: "can this number be a molecularity?" If an option offers a fractional or zero order as a molecularity, eliminate it at once. If it offers "order = molecularity" as a general rule, eliminate it too — that is true only for a one-step reaction.

9.2 Integrated rate laws and half-lives of zero- and first-order reactions

A rate law is a differential equation. Integrating it gives concentration as a function of time, which is what a question actually asks for.

Zero order

Here the rate does not depend on concentration at all, which happens when a surface or a catalyst is saturated, or in some photochemical reactions.

\text{rate} = -\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A]^0 = k

Separating and integrating from [A]_0 at t = 0 to [A] at t:

[A] = [A]_0 - kt

This is the equation of a straight line: a plot of [A] against t has slope -k and intercept [A]_0. The concentration falls by the same amount in every equal interval of time, so the reaction finishes in a finite time, t_{\text{complete}} = [A]_0/k.

Half-life. Put [A] = [A]_0/2:

\frac{[A]_0}{2} = [A]_0 - kt_{1/2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}

So for a zero-order reaction the half-life is directly proportional to the starting concentration: start with twice as much and the first half takes twice as long. Each successive half-life is shorter than the one before.

First order

\text{rate} = -\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A]

The integrated rate law of a first-order reaction

We start from the rate law and want [A] as a function of time.

Step 1 — separate the variables. Divide both sides by [A] and multiply by dt: \frac{d[A]}{[A]} = -k\,dt.

Step 2 — integrate between t = 0 (when [A] = [A]_0) and time t: \int_{[A]_0}^{[A]} \frac{d[A]}{[A]} = -k\int_0^t dt.

Step 3 — evaluate. \ln[A] - \ln[A]_0 = -kt, that is \ln\frac{[A]}{[A]_0} = -kt, or equivalently \ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt.

Step 4 — convert to base 10, because CEE data are usually given as logarithms to base 10: \ln x = 2.303\log x, so k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}.

Step 5 — exponentiate for the working form: [A] = [A]_0e^{-kt}.

Result. \ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt, [A] = [A]_0e^{-kt}, k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}.

What it means. A plot of \ln[A] against t is a straight line of slope -k; the concentration itself decays exponentially, so it never quite reaches zero. The law assumes the reaction is first order throughout and that temperature is constant.

Half-life. Put [A] = [A]_0/2:

kt_{1/2} = \ln 2 = 0.693 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}

The initial concentration has cancelled out. The half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of the starting concentration — this single sentence is the most examined idea in the chapter. After n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n:

Half-lives elapsed 1 2 3 4 5
Fraction left 1/2 1/4 1/8 1/16 1/32
Percentage left 50 % 25 % 12.5 % 6.25 % 3.13 %

The graphical test — which plot is straight?

This table answers most graph questions in the paper.

Order Plot that is a straight line Slope Intercept Half-life
0 [A] vs t -k [A]_0 [A]_0/2k, ∝ [A]_0
1 \ln[A] vs t -k \ln[A]_0 0.693/k, independent of [A]_0
2 1/[A] vs t +k 1/[A]_0 1/(k[A]_0)

Worked calculations

First order: rate constant from two concentrations

Problem. The concentration in a first-order reaction falls from 0.80 M to 0.10 M in 400 s. Find k and t_{1/2}.

Solution. \frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = \frac{0.80}{0.10} = 8, so k = \frac{2.303}{400}\log 8 = \frac{2.303 \times 0.903}{400} = \mathbf{5.2 \times 10^{-3}} s⁻¹.

Then t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{5.2 \times 10^{-3}} = \mathbf{133} s. Short cut: 0.80 → 0.10 is three halvings, so t_{1/2} = 400/3 = 133 s.

Zero order: half-life and completion time

Problem. A zero-order reaction has [A]_0 = 0.10 M and k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find t_{1/2} and the time for complete reaction.

Solution. t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} = \frac{0.10}{2(2.0 \times 10^{-3})} = \mathbf{25} s. Complete reaction means [A] = 0: t = \frac{[A]_0}{k} = \frac{0.10}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \mathbf{50} s. The second half takes 25 s — the same as the first, because the rate never changes.

Half-life traps
  • First order: t_{1/2} does not depend on [A]_0. An option saying "the half-life doubles when the initial concentration is doubled" is right only for zero order.
  • Zero order: t_{1/2} doubles when [A]_0 doubles, and the second half-life is shorter (it is half of the first) — unlike first order, where every half-life is equal.
  • "75 % complete" is two half-lives, not one and a half. 100 → 50 → 25 means 75 % has gone in 2t_{1/2}.
  • A first-order reaction never reaches 100 %. Any option with "completes at t = \ldots" for first order is wrong.

9.3 Collision theory, activation and threshold energy, the activated complex; factors affecting rate; catalysis

Collision theory

Molecules in a gas collide about 10^{10} times per second, yet most reactions are slow. Collision theory explains the gap with two filters:

\text{rate} \propto Z \times f

where Z is the collision frequency (collisions per unit volume per second) and f is the fraction of collisions that are effective.

A collision produces reaction only if (i) the molecules together carry energy at least equal to the threshold energy, and (ii) they are correctly oriented at the moment of impact.

  • Raising the concentration raises Z: more molecules in the same volume, more collisions, faster reaction.
  • Raising the temperature raises both the average speed (so Z rises slightly) and, far more importantly, f (which rises steeply). The temperature effect is therefore much larger than the concentration effect.
  • A catalyst raises f by providing a route with a lower energy demand.

Threshold energy, activation energy and the activated complex

Threshold energy, activation energy and activated complex

The threshold energy is the minimum total energy that colliding molecules must possess if they are to react.

The activation energy E_a is the extra energy the reactants must gain above their average energy to reach the threshold: E_a = E_{\text{threshold}} - E_{\text{reactants}}.

The activated complex (transition state) is the short-lived, unstable, high-energy arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy barrier; it is not an intermediate and cannot be isolated.

For a single-step reaction the enthalpy change is the difference of the two barriers:

\Delta H = E_{a(\text{forward})} - E_{a(\text{backward})}

For an exothermic reaction E_{a(\text{backward})} > E_{a(\text{forward})}; for an endothermic one the reverse.

A catalyst lowers both barriers by the same amount, so \Delta H is untouched and the equilibrium constant cannot change — only the speed with which equilibrium is reached.

Temperature and the Arrhenius equation

k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}

A is the frequency factor (roughly the collision frequency with the right orientation), E_a the activation energy in J mol⁻¹, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T the absolute temperature. Taking logarithms:

\ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{RT}

so a plot of \ln k against 1/T is a straight line of slope -E_a/R. Comparing two temperatures eliminates A:

\log\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)

Because E_a sits in the exponent, a small rise in T produces a large rise in k.

The empirical temperature coefficient is k at (T + 10) divided by k at T; for most reactions near room temperature it lies between 2 and 3, which is the familiar rule that a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate.

Arrhenius in one line

Problem. A reaction has E_a = 50 kJ mol⁻¹. By what factor does k increase when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K? (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

Solution. \log\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{50000}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left(\frac{1}{300} - \frac{1}{310}\right) = 2612 \times (1.075 \times 10^{-4}) = 0.281. \frac{k_2}{k_1} = 10^{0.281} = \mathbf{1.9}, i.e. the rate roughly doubles — the 10 °C rule, now derived rather than memorised.

What temperature does *not* do

A rise in temperature does not lower the activation energy. The barrier stays where it is; what changes is how many molecules have enough energy to clear it. An option saying "heating lowers E_a" is a standard wrong key. Only a catalyst lowers E_a.

The other factors that change the rate

Factor Effect Reason
Concentration of reactants rate rises more molecules per unit volume, so more collisions per second
Pressure (gases) rate rises with pressure same as raising concentration
Surface area (solids) rate rises with finer division reaction happens at the surface only
Temperature rate rises steeply larger fraction of molecules above E_a
Catalyst rate rises alternative path with lower E_a
Nature of the reactants ionic and radical reactions are fast; covalent bond-breaking is slow bond strength and number of bonds to break
Light starts photochemical reactions photons supply the activation energy (H₂ + Cl₂, photography, photosynthesis)
Solvent can change the rate greatly polarity and solvation stabilise or destabilise the activated complex

Catalysis: homogeneous, heterogeneous and enzyme

Catalyst

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without itself being consumed, by providing an alternative reaction path of lower activation energy. It is recovered chemically unchanged in mass and composition at the end of the reaction.

Type Phase How it works Examples
Homogeneous same phase as the reactants (usually all gas or all liquid) forms a short-lived intermediate with a reactant, which then decomposes NO in the lead-chamber process (SO₂ + O₂); H⁺ in the hydrolysis of an ester; Cl• in the destruction of ozone; I⁻ in the decomposition of H₂O₂
Heterogeneous different phase — usually a solid with gaseous or liquid reactants reactants are adsorbed on the surface, which weakens their bonds and holds them in the right orientation Fe in the Haber process; V₂O₅ in the contact process; Pt in the oxidation of SO₂ and in catalytic converters; Ni in the hydrogenation of oils; MnO₂ in the decomposition of KClO₃
Enzyme biological, in living cells a protein with an active site of fixed shape; the substrate fits like a key in a lock, so the enzyme is highly specific zymase (glucose → ethanol); invertase (sucrose → glucose + fructose); urease (urea → NH₃ + CO₂); pepsin and trypsin (proteins); catalase (H₂O₂)

Characteristics of a catalyst — the list examiners pick from.

  1. It increases the rate of the forward and the backward reaction equally, so it shortens the time to reach equilibrium but does not shift the position of equilibrium or change K, \Delta H or \Delta G.
  2. It is needed in only a small amount and is regenerated, so its mass and composition are unchanged at the end.
  3. It is highly specific: MnO₂ works for KClO₃ but not for every decomposition.
  4. It works by lowering the activation energy, not by supplying energy.
  5. A finely divided catalyst is more effective — greater surface area.
  6. A promoter increases a catalyst's activity (Mo promotes Fe in the Haber process); a poison (catalyst poison) destroys it (arsenic poisons the Pt catalyst in the contact process; lead poisons the Pt in a catalytic converter).
  7. A negative catalyst or inhibitor slows a reaction (glycerol in hydrogen peroxide; tetraethyl lead in petrol).
  8. In autocatalysis a product catalyses its own reaction (Mn²⁺ in the permanganate–oxalate titration).
  9. A catalyst cannot make a thermodynamically forbidden reaction happen; it only speeds a reaction that is already possible.
  10. Enzymes are destroyed by high temperature and by extremes of pH — they are denatured, which is why the body has an optimum temperature near 37 °C.
The three "cannot"s of a catalyst

A catalyst cannot change \Delta H, cannot change the equilibrium constant, and cannot start a reaction that is thermodynamically impossible. If an option claims any of these, it is the distractor.

Orders and units to memorise: 0 → mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; 1 → s⁻¹; 2 → L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; 3 → L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.

Order–molecularity gaps: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (order 1.5, molecularity 2); 2NH₃ on tungsten (order 0, molecularity 2); ester hydrolysis in excess water (pseudo-first-order, molecularity 2).

Chapter summary

  • Rate is positive: for a reactant rate = -(1/a)d[R]/dt; the coefficient of every species must be included. Average rate is a chord, instantaneous rate a tangent.
  • The rate law is experimental; order is the sum of the exponents and may be 0, fractional or negative, while molecularity is a theoretical whole number for one step.
  • Units of k: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (0), s⁻¹ (1), L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (2), L² mol⁻² s⁻¹ (3).
  • Zero order: [A] = [A]_0 - kt, t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k (doubles when [A]_0 doubles), and the reaction finishes at [A]_0/k.
  • First order: \ln([A]_0/[A]) = kt, [A] = [A]_0e^{-kt}, t_{1/2} = 0.693/k — independent of [A]_0; n half-lives leave (1/2)^n.
  • A straight \ln[A]–t plot (slope -k) is the test for first order; a straight [A]–t plot is the test for zero order.
  • Collision theory: rate depends on collision frequency and on the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ threshold energy and correct orientation; the activated complex is the top of the barrier.
  • k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}; a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate; the barrier itself does not fall with temperature.
  • A catalyst lowers E_a for both directions, speeds the approach to equilibrium, and changes neither \Delta H, \Delta G nor K; enzymes are specific biological catalysts with an optimum pH and temperature.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Define rate, order and molecularity. Derive the integrated rate law and half-life of a first-order reaction with a numerical. [10]

Model answer D1: rate laws and first-order kinetics (10 marks)

Introduction. The rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. For aA \to products, rate = -\dfrac1a\dfrac{d[A]}{dt}. The rate law is rate = k[A]^m[B]^n and is found only by experiment.

The order is m + n, and k is the rate constant.

Molecularity is the number of molecules colliding in an elementary step, so it is always a whole number (1, 2 or rarely 3) and has no meaning for a complex reaction, whereas order can be zero or fractional.

Order Rate law Unit of k Integrated form Half-life
Zero rate = k \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} [A] = [A]_0 - kt \dfrac{[A]_0}{2k}
First rate = k[A] \text{s}^{-1} \ln\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt \dfrac{0.693}{k}
Second rate = k[A]^2 \text{L mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} \dfrac1{[A]} - \dfrac1{[A]_0} = kt \dfrac1{k[A]_0}

Derivation (first order). -\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A], so \dfrac{d[A]}{[A]} = -k\,dt. Integrating from [A]_0 to [A]: \ln[A] - \ln[A]_0 = -kt, so [A] = [A]_0e^{-kt}, or k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]}.

The half-life is found by putting [A] = [A]_0/2: t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln2}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}, independent of the initial concentration.

Examples of first order: radioactive decay, decomposition of N₂O₅, H₂O₂, and inversion of sugar (pseudo first order, since water is in large excess). The graph of \log[A] against t is a straight line with slope -k/2.303.

Other points. (1) The slowest step is the rate-determining step. (2) For n half-lives, [A] = [A]_0/2^n. (3) The time for 99.9\% completion is about 10 half-lives.

Numerical. A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693\ \text{min}^{-1}. Then t_{1/2} = 10\ \text{min}. The time for 75\% completion is \dfrac{2.303}{0.0693}\log\dfrac{100}{25} = 20\ \text{min} (two half-lives). After 30\ \text{min} the fraction left is \tfrac18 = 12.5\%.

Conclusion. For a first-order reaction t_{1/2} = 0.693/k is constant, and order is found only by experiment.

Model answer D2: collision theory, Arrhenius equation and catalysis (10 marks)

Introduction. A reaction occurs only when molecules collide with enough energy and the correct orientation. Collisions that satisfy both are effective collisions.

Collision theory. Rate = Z_{AB}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\times P, where Z_{AB} is the collision frequency, e^{-E_a/RT} is the fraction of collisions with energy above the activation energy E_a and P is the steric factor.

Arrhenius equation. k = Ae^{-E_a/RT} or \ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}. A graph of \ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope -E_a/R. For two temperatures:

\log\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac1{T_1} - \frac1{T_2}\right)

Temperature effect. The rate of many reactions roughly doubles for a 10^{\circ}\text{C} rise, because the fraction of molecules with energy above E_a rises sharply, even though the average energy changes very little.

Catalyst. A catalyst provides an alternative path with a lower E_a, so k increases. It does not change \Delta H, \Delta G or the equilibrium constant, only the time to reach equilibrium. It is specific, and a small amount is enough.

Type Example
Homogeneous NO in the lead chamber process, H⁺ in ester hydrolysis
Heterogeneous Fe in Haber, V₂O₅ in Contact, Pt in the converter
Enzyme catalase, amylase
Autocatalysis Mn²⁺ in permanganate-oxalate
Promoter and poison Mo promotes Fe, As poisons Pt

Adsorption theory of heterogeneous catalysis: reactants adsorb on the surface, react and the products desorb.

Numerical. If the rate constant doubles from 300\ \text{K} to 310\ \text{K}: E_a = \dfrac{2.303\times8.314\times\log2\times300\times310}{10} = 53.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}.

If a catalyst lowers E_a by 10\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} at 300\ \text{K}, k increases by e^{10000/(8.314\times300)} = e^{4.01} = 55 times.

Conclusion. The rate rises with temperature because more collisions exceed E_a, and a catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering E_a without altering the equilibrium.
